summary: This round-4 diff (PROTOCOL_OWNER_AI.yaml A15/A16 rewrite, the bashrc-snippet guard, and its two test files) genuinely closes the argv-position bypass it targets and adds a plausible task-registry cross-reference for the cgroup-forgery concern, with honest disclosure of several known limitations -- but the detection layer for both git and gh still matches subcommands by literal token name only, which misses the standard, well-documented alias features of both real binaries. `git -c alias.wip=push wip origin master` (a single, self-contained command line requiring no prior setup, no root, and no exotic tooling) sets a one-shot config-based alias and invokes it in the same command: `_interactive_guard_git_find_subcommand` correctly walks past `-c alias.wip=push` as a global option pair, but then sees the literal token `wip`, not `push`, so `_interactive_guard_subcommand` never equals "push", the block is skipped, and the wrapper execs the real git with the original argv -- which real git then expands via its native alias mechanism into an actual, unblocked push to master. The identical bypass class exists on the gh side via `gh alias set` followed by invoking the alias (e.g. an alias mapped to `pr merge`), since `_interactive_guard_gh_is_merge` only recognizes the literal `pr merge` and `api` tokens. Neither vector is mentioned anywhere in this diff's own extensive 'known_limitations'/round-4 sections (which otherwise show real, live-verified rigor for the flag-position and cgroup issues), meaning this specific audit pass did not find it, and the shipped test suite has no coverage for it. Given that the entire deliverable's purpose and selling point is 'a real, technical guard that cannot be talked around,' shipping it with a still-open, textbook bypass of the exact class this task exists to close is a correctness/security gap serious enough to reject rather than approve for autonomous tier1 merge -- this should go back for a round 5 that closes native git/gh command aliasing (e.g. by rejecting/stripping `-c alias.*=` and `--config`-set aliases outright, and refusing to trust any subcommand token without first resolving effective aliases via `git config --get-regexp ^alias\.` / `gh alias list`).
issues: Git-alias bypass: `git -c alias.<name>=push <name> <remote> <branch>` (or a pre-existing `[alias]` entry in ~/.gitconfig) lets an interactive session push to a protected branch completely undetected, because `_interactive_guard_git_find_subcommand` matches on the literal subcommand token and has no alias-resolution step; the wrapper execs the real git with the untouched argv, and real git expands the alias into an actual push.

Gh-alias bypass: the same class applies to `gh alias set <name> 'pr merge ...'` followed by `gh <name> ...` -- `_interactive_guard_gh_is_merge` only recognizes the literal `pr merge` / `api ... /pulls/*/merge` forms and has no alias-resolution step, so an aliased merge command passes through unblocked.

Neither bypass is disclosed in this diff's own (otherwise thorough) known_limitations sections, and neither has a regression-test scenario in tests/interactive_session_guard_test.sh, indicating this round's audit did not consider git/gh's native command-aliasing feature at all despite it being a standard, non-exotic capability of both tools.
